introduction: On this fifth Sunday of Easter, Jesus says, I am the vine, you are the branches. Apart from him we can do nothing; remaining in him, we bear much fruit. In the first reading, Barnabas welcomes Saul, the former persecutor, into the community. John reminds us to love not only in word but in deed and truth. Let us remain in Christ, so that our lives may bear fruit for others.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, we are branches of the true vine. Let us bring our prayers to the Father, the vinedresser.
intentions: For the Church: that, remaining in Christ, she may bear much fruit of holiness and charity in the world. Let us pray to the Lord.
For new converts and those returning to the faith: that they may be welcomed by Christian communities, as Barnabas welcomed Saul. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who feel their lives are fruitless or wasted: that they may discover that God can still bring life from them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who suffer pruning through illness, loss or failure: that they may trust the Father's care and grow stronger in faith. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may love one another not only in word but in deed and truth. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Father, you are the vinedresser, and your Son is the true vine. Keep us united to him, prune what is fruitless in us, and let our lives give you glory. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Remain in me
reflection.body:
Jesus uses a simple image that anyone who has seen a vineyard can understand: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer." A branch cut off from the vine dries up. A branch joined to it is full of life and fruit.

The word he repeats is remain. "Remain in me, and I in you." And the reason is plain: "I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing." Christian life is not first of all a list of tasks. It is staying connected to Christ, through prayer, the sacraments and his word.

Jesus also speaks of pruning: "Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit." Pruning hurts. But a gardener prunes because he wants more fruit, not because he wants to harm the plant. Some of the hard seasons in our lives can be seen in that light.

The first reading shows a branch newly grafted onto the vine. Saul, who had persecuted the Church, tries to join the disciples in Jerusalem, "but they were all afraid of him." It is Barnabas who takes him by the hand and vouches for him. Without Barnabas, we might never have had Saint Paul.

John tells us what the fruit looks like: "let's not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth." And he offers a word of comfort for anxious consciences: "God is greater than our heart, and knows all things."

This week, ask yourself where you are drawing your strength from. Make a small, fixed time each day to remain with the Lord. And look for someone who, like Saul, needs a Barnabas: someone new, or someone others are wary of, who needs a welcome.
